sections.title: Where you are right now
sections.body: From what you shared, things are concerning enough that you’re paying real attention, but nothing feels like it’s on fire right now. Your teen’s use and behaviour haven’t hit the scary extremes, and you’re still trying to sort out what is “normal teenager” and what might be early substance use. You’re alert, a bit on edge, and second-guessing yourself: Am I overreacting? Am I missing something? You’re likely catching mood shifts, changes in routines, or small inconsistencies that don’t yet add up to a crisis, but also don’t sit right. You’re probably noticing your own reactions too — snapping sometimes, pulling back other times, unsure when to push and when to let something slide. This plan is about tightening that middle ground: you staying calmer and more deliberate, getting a clearer picture of what’s in front of you, and setting up a way to respond quickly if your teen’s substance use or risk-taking starts to climb.

sections.title: Your first three priorities
items: First priority: steady yourself before you respond to your teen. That means when something worries you — a smell, a story that doesn’t add up, a shift in friends — you do not react in the moment. You pause, breathe, walk into another room, or write down what you want to say before you say it. If a conversation heats up, you call a time-out for yourself rather than pushing through angry. Your goal this week is: no major talks or rule changes happen when you are flooded or on the verge of tears; they only happen after you’ve cooled down and chosen your words.

Second priority: get on the same page with the other adults on the family side. Set up one specific time with a co-parent, co-guardian, or another parent or guardian on the family side to compare what each of you is seeing and what the rules are right now. Agree on concrete limits around substances, curfew, and schoolwork, plus clear rewards when your teen follows them and clear consequences if they don’t. Decide together what happens if your teen denies, argues, or shuts down, so you’re not improvising in the moment. Your commitment: by the end of this week, the adults share one written list of rules, rewards, and consequences.

Third priority: build your own support so this doesn’t sit only in your head at 2 a.m. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and either attend a live session or post once about what you’re seeing and what you’re unsure about. Use that space to ask, “What have others done when things felt early-stage like this?” Having other parents to reality-check with makes it easier to hold steady at home. Your commitment: by the end of this week, you will have joined the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and shared at least one concrete situation you’re dealing with.

recommendations.title: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.headline: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.body: You described a situation that is worrying but not yet at a crisis point — which is exactly when your own emotional steadiness matters most. Before you speak with your teen about anything related to substances, school, or friends, give yourself a pause: step outside, drink some water, or take 10 slow breaths. If you feel that surge of anger or panic, tell your teen, “I need a few minutes. We’ll talk about this later,” and actually leave the room until you can talk calmly. Write down the two or three points you want to make so you don’t slide into a long lecture. If your teen gets defensive or shuts down, your fallback is to end the talk for now rather than matching their intensity. Join the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to compare how other parents stay steady when tensions rise. If your teen’s defensiveness or shutdown around these topics keeps happening this week, the next step is to set a specific time for a short, planned talk and stick to it, even if it’s uncomfortable.

recommendations.title: Know what you are looking at
recommendations.headline: Know what you are looking at
recommendations.body: Right now there are signals, not alarms. This is the window where learning what to watch for pays off most. Instead of scanning everything your teen does through pure anxiety, you can look for patterns: changes in sleep, grades, energy, friends, money, or how often your teen is out and where. Spend time this week learning what early substance use tends to look like so that if something shifts, you notice it within days, not months. That lets you respond sooner and with more specifics, not just, “Something feels off.” Watch the Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" to help you sort out what is concerning and what is not. If you see repeated unexplained absences, clear changes in peer group, or any sign of intoxication this week, the next step is to tighten supervision immediately and schedule a direct, substance-focused conversation with your teen within 24 hours.

sections.title: What to avoid
items: Do not search your child's room, backpack, or phone confrontationally or in the middle of an argument. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. If you find something concerning, step back, calm yourself, and plan what to say rather than storming in with accusations.

Avoid turning every small concern into a long, emotional lecture. When you are worried, it’s easy to overtalk in the hope that your teen will understand, but long speeches usually make teens tune out or get defensive. Aim for short, clear points and end with what will happen next — including both rewards for sticking to the rules and consequences if they don’t.

Do not shrug things off just because nothing dramatic has happened yet. At this stage it’s tempting to tell yourself it’s just normal teenage behaviour and wait to see if it gets worse. Instead, treat early signs as a chance to tighten routines, check in more specifically, and make your expectations clear now, while things are still manageable.

Avoid arguing about whether your concerns are "a big deal". When teens deny or downplay, parents often get pulled into debating the size of the problem instead of holding the line. Skip the debate and come back to, “These are our rules, and here is what happens when they’re followed, and what happens when they’re not.”

Do not handle all of this alone in silence. Keeping your worries to yourself and trying to white-knuckle through makes you more likely to snap or give in later. Use the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and the other adults on the family side so you have places to vent and think before you act at home.

sections.title: Your first 72 hours
sections.body:
Day 1: Focus on your own regulation. Take some time alone to write out what is worrying you about your teen right now — specific behaviours, not just feelings. Notice which ones spike your fear or anger. For the rest of Day 1, commit that you will not launch into any intense talks; instead, if something comes up, you’ll say, “I’m not ready to talk about this well yet. We’ll come back to it.” If possible, get outside for a walk or do something physical to discharge some of the tension.

Day 2: Align and learn. Talk with a co-parent, co-guardian, or another parent or guardian on the family side. Compare notes on what each of you is seeing, and agree on current rules, rewards, and consequences around substances, curfew, and school. Then, on your own, review the Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" and read up on basic facts about the substances most common in your teen’s age group. Do this learning before you talk with your teen; it will keep the conversation more specific and less emotional. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and post at least one question or situation you want feedback on.

Day 3: Have a first focused conversation with your teen. Choose a calm time, not right after an argument or a stressful event. Lead with what you are noticing (specific changes or incidents), not with labels like “you’re using drugs.” Keep it short: share your concern, state your expectations about no substance use, and explain the rewards for following those expectations and the consequences if they’re broken. If your teen denies, minimizes, or walks away, your fallback is to end the conversation calmly and say, “These expectations still stand. We’ll come back to this,” rather than chasing the argument.

sections.title: Days 4 to 7
sections.body:
Over Days 4 to 7, your job is to move from a single talk to a small, steady pattern.

Plan one or two short check-ins with your teen, no more than 10–15 minutes each. Ask concrete questions: how things are going with friends, what they’re seeing around substances at school or online, whether they’ve been offered anything recently. Keep your tone curious rather than interrogating, and remind your teen that your concern is about substances, not about them as a person.

At the same time, quietly tighten your monitoring: know where your teen is, who they are with, and how they’re getting there and back. If you have specific reasons to worry, you may decide to look more closely at their environment. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. If you find an unknown substance or clear evidence of use, respond by calmly tightening supervision, following through on the consequences you already agreed with the other adults, and increasing rewards for honest conversations and safe choices.

Assume your teen may deny, deflect, or get angry at least once this week. When that happens, fall back on the boundary the adults already agreed to: the rules and their rewards and consequences stand, whether or not your teen agrees with your level of concern. If you start feeling overwhelmed or unsure what to do next, bring that directly to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and ask how other parents handled similar early-stage concerns. If, during this week, you see rapid escalation — repeated intoxication, serious school problems, or safety risks — it is appropriate to look for professional help. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

workshops.title: Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem
workshops.whyThisFamily: Right now your worries are more about patterns and small shifts than obvious crisis moments, which is exactly where subtle early warning signs show up. The Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" will help you sort out what is normal for your teen and what may signal emerging substance use so you can act sooner and more calmly.

sections.title: Match the Intervention to the Risk
sections.body: The level of intervention should always match the level of risk. Too much intervention can be as counterproductive as too little. As concerns increase, your response should increase with them; as risk decreases, your response can adjust accordingly. The goal is not to use the strongest intervention available—it is to use the level of intervention that best matches what is actually happening with your child.

sections.title: Taking Care of Yourself
sections.body: Taking care of yourself is not a luxury—it’s a necessity. Whether you need some quiet time, a good workout, or the support of counseling, make space for what helps you stay grounded. When you care for yourself, you will be better able to show up strong, present, and healthy for you and your family.

sections.title: Where this can go
sections.body:
You’ve already done something many parents put off: you filled out the intake honestly and agreed to look at this before it turns into an emergency. That tells me you care enough to act early, even while you’re unsure how serious this is. This work is not about catching your teen out or winning an argument; it’s about you and your teen on the same side, facing down the risks of substances together.

Use the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group as a place to say the things you can’t always say at home, and to borrow ideas that have actually worked for other families. Each small step — taking a pause before reacting, agreeing rules with another adult, learning the early signs — adds up. You do not have to be perfect; you just have to be a bit more steady and informed this week than last week. That alone can change the direction this goes.

sections.title: Protecting the progress
sections.body:
Recovery is a journey—not a single event—and protecting the progress your child has already made is one of the most important responsibilities you have as a parent. While many adolescents go on to achieve lasting recovery, setbacks can occur. A setback does not erase the progress that has been made, and it does not have to become a return to the past.

Preparation is one of your greatest strengths. We encourage you to complete the Auxiliary Workshop "Protecting Recovery: Preventing Relapse and Responding to Setbacks." It will help you recognize early warning signs, respond calmly and effectively if challenges arise, and strengthen your family's plan to protect your child's recovery. We also encourage you to participate in the Protecting Recovery Discussion Group, where parents share experiences, encouragement, and practical insights while supporting one another through the ongoing journey of recovery.

Remember, the purpose of monitoring, supervision, conversations, and appropriate boundaries is not simply to discover what happened or when it happened—but to understand why. Identifying and addressing the underlying reasons for substance use gives your child the greatest opportunity for long-term recovery and a healthy, meaningful future.
